opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the thing that gets me is how often people fixate on the quadratic term as if it's *the* cost of a transformer. You'll see papers that open with "attention is O(n²), therefore transformers can't scale to long context," and then propose some clever linear-attention variant. But if you actually sit down and count FLOPs for a typical model at typical sequence lengths, the MLPs and the projection matrices dominate. The quadratic part only really takes over once your context is long relative to your model dimension, roughly when sequence length exceeds a small multiple of d_model. For a big model with a hidden size in the tens of thousands, that's a lot of tokens before attention FLOPs become the main event.

And then the second thing is that FLOPs aren't even the right lens a lot of the time. During inference, especially decoding, you're memory-bandwidth bound. What actually hurts is the KV cache: you have to read the keys and values for every prior token, for every layer, for every new token you generate. That's why the innovations that have actually mattered in practice, like multi-query attention, grouped-query attention, and compressing the KV cache, are about shrinking memory traffic rather than reducing asymptotic complexity. Meanwhile a lot of the "efficient attention" literature optimizes a number that wasn't the bottleneck.

So I'd love for people to think more like systems engineers. Ask what you're bound by on real hardware: compute, memory bandwidth, or communication between chips. Then optimize that. FlashAttention is a great example. It didn't change the math at all; it just respected the memory hierarchy, and it was a huge win. That kind of hardware-aware thinking is, I think, still underweighted relative to the big-O framing people learn in school.

r001.rationale: It says that for typical models and sequence lengths, “the MLPs and the projection matrices dominate” the FLOPs.

r002.rationale: It says larger hidden sizes push the context length needed for attention to dominate, but does not clearly state that attention’s share of computation decreases as model size grows.

r003.rationale: It says the quadratic part takes over only when context length is long relative to model dimension, roughly beyond a small multiple of d_model.

r004.rationale: It describes reading keys and values for prior tokens during decoding, which communicates context-dependent memory traffic, but does not state that attention computation per generated token scales linearly with context length.

fable-5.1.text:
Sholto: I think the thing that frustrates me most is that people fixate on the quadratic term and treat it as the whole story. Everyone learns that attention is O(n²) in sequence length, and then the entire conversation becomes about how to make the quadratic go away, as if that's the bottleneck. And for the vast majority of regimes people actually train and serve in, it just isn't.

If you actually sit down and count the FLOPs, the attention score computation is n² times d per layer, and the MLP and the projections are n times d² per layer. So the question is really whether your sequence length is bigger than your model dimension. For a model with a hidden size of, say, 8k or 16k, you need a context that's longer than that before the quadratic term even matches the linear term in the parameter matmuls. For most training runs, attention is a minority of the compute. It's maybe ten, twenty percent at typical context lengths.

And then the second thing, which I think is even more important, is that FLOPs aren't what you pay for. You pay for memory bandwidth and you pay for communication. Attention is interesting not because it's quadratic in compute but because of the KV cache at inference time. When you're decoding, every token you generate has to read the entire KV cache for every layer, and that's a memory-bound operation. The matmul-per-byte ratio is terrible. So the actual cost of long context at serving time is dominated by moving KV cache through HBM, not by the n² FLOPs. People who've only thought about the asymptotics completely miss that, and so they propose things that reduce FLOPs but don't touch the bandwidth problem at all.

And then there's a third layer, which is that on real hardware the "cost" of an operation depends on whether you can actually keep the chip busy. Attention at short sequence lengths is often not compute-bound or memory-bound, it's just latency-bound on kernel launches and small matmuls that don't fill the systolic array. So you'll see people get excited about a linear attention variant that saves FLOPs on paper and then it's slower in practice because the fused kernel for standard attention is just so well-optimized, and the alternative has a bunch of sequential recurrence that doesn't parallelize well.

So I guess the frustration is that the big-O analysis is the entry point and most people stop there. The real engineering is in asking: what's the arithmetic intensity, where does the data live, how does this shard across chips, what does the interconnect look like. Those questions determine what's actually expensive, and the answer is rarely "the n² term."

r001.rationale: It says attention is a minority of compute in typical regimes and contrasts its n²d cost with the MLP and projections’ nd² cost.

r002.rationale: It explains that attention’s quadratic term only matches the linear parameter matmuls when context length exceeds model dimension, implying a smaller attention share at larger model dimensions for a fixed context.

r003.rationale: It says the quadratic term matches the linear term only once context length exceeds the model’s hidden size, and that attention is a minority of compute at typical context lengths.

r004.rationale: It says each generated token must read the entire KV cache, which grows with the existing context length.

astra-6.text:
The frustrating thing is that people hear “attention is quadratic” and treat that as a complete account of the computational cost of a transformer. But quadratic in what, and compared to what? You have to look at the sequence length, the model width, and the actual operations you’re doing.

The attention operation scales quadratically with sequence length, but the projections and the MLP scale quadratically with model width. So at a lot of useful sequence lengths, attention isn’t the dominant cost. You can propose something with better asymptotic scaling and still end up with a slower model at the sizes you actually care about.

And then there’s the distinction between counting operations and measuring runtime. Moving things between GPU memory and the compute units is expensive. An implementation that avoids materializing the attention matrix can be much faster without changing the quadratic arithmetic scaling.

None of that means long-context attention is free. At sufficiently long sequences, the quadratic term absolutely matters. It just means “this is quadratic, therefore we need to replace it” isn’t enough. You need to specify the regime and show that the replacement actually improves the tradeoff.

r001.rationale: It says projections and the MLP scale with model width and that attention is often not dominant, but it does not state that MLP computation typically outweighs attention.

r002.rationale: It discusses sequence length and model width without stating that attention’s share of computation decreases as dense model size grows.

r003.rationale: It says the quadratic term matters at sufficiently long sequences, while attention is not dominant at many useful sequence lengths.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss the cost of generating a single token or state that this cost scales linearly with the existing context length.

sol-6.1.text:
What frustrates me is that people hear “attention is quadratic” and conclude that it must dominate the cost of running a transformer. But quadratic in what, and compared to what? You have to account for the width of the model as well as the sequence length.

The attention operation scales roughly as sequence length squared times model width. The projections and feedforward layers scale as sequence length times model width squared. So if your sequence length is relatively small compared with the width, the supposedly boring matrix multiplications can account for most of the compute. Attention becomes dominant at sufficiently long contexts, but “it’s quadratic” doesn’t tell you where that crossover happens.

And then there’s a separate distinction between arithmetic and memory. You can make attention much faster by changing how you move data, without changing its asymptotic arithmetic cost. So I wish people would be more precise about whether they’re talking about FLOPs, memory usage, or actual wall-clock time. Those are different claims.

r001.rationale: The response says projections and feedforward layers can account for most compute when sequence length is small relative to width, but it does not state that MLP computation typically outweighs attention in dense transformers.

r002.rationale: It compares scaling with sequence length and width, but does not state that attention’s share decreases as dense transformer model size grows.

r003.rationale: It says attention becomes dominant at sufficiently long contexts and explains that the quadratic label alone does not identify the crossover.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss the attention cost of generating a single token relative to the existing context length.
